newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: France throws spanner into single currency works.
newsitem.headline: France throws spanner into single currency works.

text.p: France threw the European Union's plans for a single currency into confusion on Monday when it asked for time to study a previously agreed pact to keep budget deficits tight after the currency is launched.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told his EU counterparts at a meeting in Luxembourg that Paris needed time to study the bloc's stability pact, an integral part of its plans for economic and monetary union (EMU).
The pact, agreed after hard-fought overnight negotiations in Dublin in December, was supposed to be ratified by EU leaders when they meet in Amsterdam next week.
Strauss-Kahn's move triggered a scramble to find a compromise that could paper over the problem and allow for a successful summit.
European Commission President Jacques Santer was to go to Paris on Thursday to see new French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin with a proposal, EU sources said.

The idea was for the EU to come up with a resolution that would meet France's concerns that the stability pact did not do enough for employment and at the same time allow the bloc to show that EMU was on track.
"A text will be prepared for Amsterdam," outgoing Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn said. But he added later to Reuters: "France's position is pushing us all too far."
Other sources indicated, there was little expectation that the pact could be signed at Amsterdam, even if a declaration was agreed.

Strauss-Kahn, kicking off his debut as finance minister with a bang, said it would take more than a week for Paris to consider the stability pact, which France wants to be amended with an attachment on employment.
Officials said Strauss-Kahn had said the new French government wanted to discuss the plan with the National Assembly and could not do so until June 19, two days after the Amsterdam summit.
Financial markets initially reacted sharply to the news, with the mark leaping against other European currencies, then settling down.
"It's not the end of EMU in itself, but it's not helping," said Neal Kimberly of Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
Any hint of an unravelling of the EU's plans for a single currency adds fuel to the belief of some in the market that EMU may have to be delayed from its January 1, 1999 start date.
EU ministers and officials rushed to portray the French move as a momentary blip, a not-unreasonable desire by a new government to look at what its predecessor had agreed.
"There was a great deal of sympathy for the French position," Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm, chairman of the meeting, said.

Strauss-Kahn said France did not want to reopen the agreement on the pact, which could lead to fines on countries running excessive deficits, but he clearly indicated Paris was not happy with the current deal.
"We're not seeking to renegotiate the stability pact, but we cannot approve it today," he told a news conference. France also reiterated France's desire to see EMU start on time.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, himself recently at the centre of a storm over plans to revalue German gold reserves to help meet the economic targets for EMU tests, was adamant the plan would not unravel.
"What has been agreed upon and discussed for two years can no longer be put up for negotiation," Waigel told reporters.

France's insistence on an addendum to the pact to spell out how EU countries will coordinate economic policy after the launch of the euro was also seen threatening the ability of the 15-nation EU to agree a new treaty at the Amsterdam summit.
Part of the treaty negotiations include discussion of adopting a so-called Employment Chapter to make job creation a formal EU priority.
The two were seen as linked by some EU officials.

The French demand for time to consider the stability pact follows a fortnight in which the bloc's plans for the currency have come under intense pressure, in part because of the French election and in part because of Bonn's fiscal difficulties.
Waigel's plan to plug a gaping hole in Bonn's 1997 revenues by revaluing the Bundesbank's gold reserves left him politically weakened and accused of trying to cook the books for EMU.
But he remained determined as ever on Monday to argue that governments must bring their 1997 deficits down to three percent of gross domestic product -- the EMU target.
"Whoever says 3.3 percent will in the end land at more than four percent...(which to me) is not acceptable," he told reporters.
In Germany, Chancellor Helmut Kohl put a bright face on his country's prospects, saying the government's target of 2.5 percent growth for the full year was attainable.
